title: Always Honor the Past Before Explaining What's Next
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that leaders undermine their own change efforts by rushing to announce a new vision before properly closing out the old one. It frames transition as an emotional process in which people need to let go of a past effort — into which they invested careers, reputations, and relationships — before they can genuinely commit to what comes next. The author insists that honoring the past is not a symbolic nicety but a psychological prerequisite for closure, and that this matters even more when a transition follows failure or a leader's departure. Crucially, the piece argues that even unsuccessful past efforts contain something worth honoring — lessons learned, skills built, relationships forged, values demonstrated — and that specificity in acknowledging this makes people more likely to feel their contributions mattered. The core warning is that leaders who skip this step get teams that are still mentally processing the past and therefore unable to fully commit to the future, meaning the pause to honor what came before is the foundation the next chapter must stand on.

quotes: Amid change and transition, people go through an emotional stage of letting go of the old before they can commit to the new. Leaders who miss this essentially ask people to break ground on something new before they’ve finished with what came before.
They recognize that people were invested in the last effort. Team members showed up for it, staked their careers and reputations on it, and built relationships around it.

Honoring the past before diving into the next thing provides definitive closure and allows people to feel good about their efforts. This is even more important if the transition to a new objective follows a failure or a leader’s departure.

Even when the past effort didn’t achieve its goal, leaders can find something worth honoring in it. Lessons learned, skills acquired or sharpened, relationships forged along the way, and values demonstrated are prime examples.

This step isn’t a courtesy. It’s the foundation the next chapter will stand on. Leaders who skip it will likely find distracted team members still processing what came before and unable to fully commit to what lies ahead.
